stem: Grady most likely delivered this address to the New England Society of New York in order to

options.text: persuade Northern voters to support new civil rights laws for Black Southerners
options.misconception: Grady’s pitch was about civil rights laws.

options.text: warn Northern industrialists that Southern competition would soon destroy their businesses
ask Congress to send federal troops back into the South
options.misconception: Grady wanted Reconstruction and federal troops restored.

options.text: win Northern businessmen’s investment and confidence in a reconciled South

rationales.A: The speech says nothing about civil rights laws; its subject is reconciliation and industry.
rationales.B: Grady courts Northern businessmen as guests; he does not threaten them.
rationales.C: Background: federal troops had already left the South in 1877, and Grady, a voice of reconciliation, would not ask for their return.
rationales.D: Grady speaks to New York businessmen as a guest, praises union and freedom, and paints a South open for business. His audience and his message point to one purpose: convincing Northern capital that the South is a safe, profitable place to invest.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who is listening. Grady addresses the New England Society of New York, a room of Northern businessmen.
2. Ask what he offers them. A South of “union and freedom” with “a diversified industry,” a region open for business.
3. Test the other purposes. He never mentions civil rights laws, troops, or threats to Northern firms.
4. Match the pitch. Background: Grady’s “New South” creed promised that Northern capital and Southern industry would profit together.
Remember: a speaker’s purpose hides in his audience and his promises, not only in his topic.

stimulus.source_note: Henry W. Grady, “The New South,” address to the New England Society of New York, December 1886. Grady opens by quoting Benjamin H. Hill (1866). Portrait: Henry W. Grady, Library of Congress.
stimulus.text:
[Grady opens by quoting Benjamin H. Hill, 1866:]

“There was a South of slavery and secession — that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom — that South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour.”

“The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy, the oligarchs leading in the popular movement; a social system compact and closely knitted, less splendid on the surface, but stronger at the core; a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.”

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain speech with a Library of Congress portrait
